review.material: Author-hosted paper: introduction and the sections on continuity, reversibility and recognition.
review.limitations: The central arguments and illustrative cases were reviewed; the full technical case classification has not been independently verified.

evidence.description: Rule application and compatible descriptions of successive shapes.
Loss of overlap information and requirements for reversing a change.
Geometric constraints on recognizing rule instances.

sections.title: In brief
sections.text: Spatial change is examined through three connected questions: can successive descriptions remain compatible, can a change be reversed, and can the part to change be recognized? Shape arithmetic links these questions.

sections.title: The question
sections.text: What must a computational description preserve when a rule removes an embedded part and adds another? Geometry alone can conceal the distinctions needed to explain or reverse a computation.

sections.title: Main idea or claim
sections.text: A rule application can be written S − t(A) + t(B), but its structural description, reversibility and recognition conditions require separate analysis. Fused geometry does not automatically retain its construction history.

sections.title: How the work approaches it
sections.text: The authors work with shape algebras and products, introduce compatible finite part descriptions for continuity, analyze inverse changes algebraically, and classify geometric configurations by the constraints they impose on transformations.

sections.title: Evidence and examples
sections.text: Support comes from equations, geometric cases and architectural illustrations, including emergent readings of a Leonardo plan. It is a formal investigation, rather than a statistical evaluation of design users.

sections.title: What comes out of it
sections.text: Continuity concerns relations between chosen descriptions. Reversing the arrow is insufficient when overlap has erased provenance; recording the relevant overlap information can support reversal. Recognition depends on the freedoms remaining after geometric constraints are imposed.

sections.title: Limits to keep in mind
sections.text: Topological continuity here does not mean smooth animation. A history-based undo operation is also different from proving a rule globally invertible. The exact algebra and host-shape conditions determine which claims apply.

sections.title: What to take from it
sections.text: When designing a shape system, keep geometry, the interpretation of its parts, and its recorded history distinct. Each answers a different question about the same visible change.
